Blueprint Thesis: Fluidic Warp Drive (FWD) Powered by FSUFT-U 6.0
Abstract
The Fluidic Warp Drive (FWD) is a theoretical propulsion system designed to manipulate spacetime as a 10-
dimensional quantum fluid, as described by the Fluid Spacetime Unification Field Theory - UNIFIED (FSUFT-U 6.0). 
This blueprint reimagines the FWD from its FSUFT-U 2.0 origins, integrating advanced mathematics to achieve a 
velocity of (0.1c) (10% the speed of light) within 10 seconds for a 100-meter spherical spacecraft. The design 
leverages a scalar field Φ, viscosity 𝜂eff, and compact dimensions to power and cool the system, offering a unified 
approach to interstellar travel. This thesis provides a mathematical foundation, functional description, and 
preliminary cost estimate, positioning the FWD as a testable prototype for future exploration.
1. Design Specifications
Ship: Spherical, diameter 100m, mass 𝑀ship=106kg.
Hull: Surface area 𝐴=4𝜋(50)2=31,415.9m2, acts as a radiator with a maximum temperature of 3,000K 
(tungsten-based).
FWD Bubble: Radius 110m, induces static 𝑔=9.8m/s2 locally, accelerates to 𝑣=0.1𝑐=3×107m/s in 𝑡=10s.
Power Source: 840 NFNB (Nano-Fluidic Nuclear Boost) units, each 10m3, mass 18,715kg.
Cooling: Hull radiation plus spacetime viscosity dissipation.

3. Description of Function
3.1 Operational Principle
The FWD manipulates spacetime as a 10D quantum fluid, creating a "bubble" of distorted spacetime around the 
ship. The scalar field Φ, with baseline tension Φ0≈3.99×1015GeV, is perturbed by 840 NFNB units, generating 𝛿Φ. 
This perturbation warps the fluid’s curvature (𝑅10) and flow, propelling the ship by contracting spacetime ahead 
and expanding it behind—akin to an Alcubierre drive but grounded in FSUFT-U 6.0’s fluid dynamics.
3.2 Propulsion Process
Initiation: NFNB units amplify Φ within the 110-meter bubble, requiring 1018W.
Acceleration: The bubble accelerates the ship to (0.1c) in 10 seconds, maintaining a local 𝑔=9.8m/s2 for crew 
comfort.
Heat Management: The hull radiates 9.67×1017W at 2,920K, supplemented by 𝜂eff-driven dissipation into the 
compact dimensions.
3.3 Advantages
Unified physics integration (gravity, forces, energy flow).
Compact design via 10 D energy channeling.
Viscosity-aided cooling, reducing external radiator needs.

4. Cost Analysis (Speculative, 2025 Basis)
4.1 Assumptions
Costs are speculative, based on current advanced tech (e.g., nuclear fusion, spacecraft construction), adjusted 
for theoretical exotic components.
Currency: 2025 USD, assuming moderate inflation from 2023.
4.2 Breakdown
Hull Construction:
Material: Tungsten alloy (3,000K tolerance), 31,415.9m2, 1cm thick.
Volume: 314.16m3, density ∼19,250kg/m3, mass ∼6,047tons.
Cost: $500/kg (advanced alloy fabrication), ∼$3.02billion.
NFNB Units:
840 units, each 18,715kg, total mass 15,720tons.
Cost: $10,000/kg (exotic tech akin to fusion reactors), ∼$157.2billion.
Scalar Field Generators:
Hypothetical Φ-amplification tech, ∼$50billion (R&D + prototyping).

∼$217.67billion.

The FWD, powered by FSUFT-U 6.0, is a theoretically viable propulsion system, achieving (0.1c) with 1018W via 840 
NFNB units. Its mathematics unifies spacetime manipulation with heat dissipation, leveraging 10D fluid dynamics. 
Functionally, it offers a novel interstellar travel mechanism, though its $432.89billion cost reflects the frontier nature 
of the tech. Future work includes prototyping NFNB units and testing 𝛿Φ effects, aligning with FSUFT-U 6.0’s 
empirical validation (e.g., LISA, SKA).
